## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**

*Andrew J*. *Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D*. *Auld*

Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.

ACorresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au

*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D*. *excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T*. *speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D*. *excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T*. *speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D*. *excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m2 and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T*. *speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.

Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D*. *excelsa*) or 3 m (*T*. *speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T*. *speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.

For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D*. *excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T*. *speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D*. *excelsa* (two sites) and *T*. *speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T*. *speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.

#### **Introduction**

In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and nonleguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).

However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 

{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.

Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X*. *fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T*. *speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.

In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).

In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.

#### **Methods**

#### *Study species*

*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).

*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.

#### *Sites*

Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D*. *excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E*. *sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T*. *speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E*. *sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).

All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D*. *excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.

#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*

Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D*. *excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T*. *speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact

{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T*. *speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D*. *excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T*. *speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D*. *excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m2 ).

To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T*. *speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.

#### *Primary seed dispersal*

The seeds of *D*. *excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T*. *speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T*. *speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D*. *excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.

The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D*. *excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T*. *speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D*. *excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D*. *excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T*. *speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.

#### *Seed predation*

The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:

(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.

(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.

Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.

The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.

Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D*. *excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T*. *speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.

#### *Seedling dispersal*

The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:

(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T*. *speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.

(b) for *D*. *excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T*. *speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.

#### *Analyses*

To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D*. *excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m2 were compared in *D*. *excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T*. *speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).

To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation 

{4}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.

At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D*. *excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D*. *excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T*. *speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).

We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T*. *speciosissima*. In *D*. *excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T*. *speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.

For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).

To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.

(i) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodnessof-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).

(ii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1 and *T*. *speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D*. *excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T*. *speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T*. *speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.

(iii) For *D*. *excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D*. *excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.

#### **Results**

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

For both *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D*. *excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T*. *speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T*. *speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.

#### *Fruit and seed production*

In *D*. *excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m–2) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m–2) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T*. *speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*1,2 = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*1,2 = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T*. *speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T*. *speciosissima* (*F*1,46 = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D*. *excelsa* (*F*1,42 = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D*. *excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*1,2 = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T*. *speciosissima* between sites (*F*1,2 = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*2,2 = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). In the first post-fire fruiting year (1996), the estimated density of seeds

{5}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

produced was 1.1 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> at both sites (Table 3). Seed production was higher in the second fruiting year at Site 2, but lower at Site 1. Despite the lack of significance of a year effect in the analysis, at both sites seed production declined dramatically by the third fruiting year (1997) and no seeds were produced in subsequent years (Table 1). Total post-fire seed production by *D*. *excelsa* was considerably greater than by *T*. *speciosissima* (e.g. 9.9 *v*. 2.0 seeds per m<sup>2</sup> , 2350 *v*. 430 seeds per flowering plant for *D*. *excelsa* and *T*. *speciosissima*, respectively, at Site 1) (Table 3).

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

#### *Abstract*

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

#### **Introduction**

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

#### **Methods**

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*

In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring

3	# **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria**
4	
5	*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*
6	
7	School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.
8	
9	#### *Abstract*
10	
11	Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.
12	
13	### **Introduction**
14	
15	In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.
16	
17	The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km<sup>2</sup> and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.
18	
19	Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km<sup>2</sup>) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km<sup>2</sup>) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. 234

236	
237	In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata.* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.
238	
239	The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.
240	
241	The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea.* Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa, Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea,* may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).
242	
243	The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer *(Axis porcinus)* are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.
244	
245	It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata,* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea, Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

# **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria**

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

#### *Abstract*

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

### **Introduction**

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km<sup>2</sup> and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km<sup>2</sup>) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km<sup>2</sup>) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. E. obliqua is usually regarded as relatively fire resistant by virtue of its thick bark, it may be rendered susceptible if bark is depleted by repeated burning. Widespread introgression of this species with the thinner-barked E. regnans has resulted in trees with deciduous bark on the trunk and main branches; hence in many of the wetter sites, *E. obliqua* behaves as a fire-sensitive species (Smith 1970; Ashton 1981). Recent fires in the area (1927, 1939 and 1951) have produced a mosaic pattern of regeneration of the eucalypts and could have led to the development of scrub where the fires overlapped within the early non-flowering stage of the eucalypts, or where eucalypt death occurred at a time of meagre storage of capsules in the canopy, such as has occurred at Tidal River at times during the decade 1975-85. Extremely dense regeneration of *A. verticillata* in Lilly Pilly Gully followed the fires of 1951. Four years later this scrub was 2-3 m tall and virtually impenetrable. After 10 years *A. verticillata* was mature and 4-5 m tall (Fig. 2a), but after 20 years it had begun to senesce (Fig. 2b). Death of stands commenced on the lower slopes and warmer aspects and by 1979-80 most stands were dead (Fig. 2c). The stems of the degenerating acacias were infested with numerous wood boring beetles, including *Notoceresium elongata* McKeown, *Pentarthrium australe* McKeown and *Menephilus coerulescens* Haag. It is possible that these and other insects have been responsible for the hastened decline of this even-aged generation. In 1978, regeneration from soil-stored seed of *A. verticillata* and *G. ovata* was occurring in open areas between patches of *G. ovata, Pteridium esculentum* and *T. juncea*. On the upper slopes, shrubs of *Kunzea ambigua* had invaded much of the degenerate scrub, whilst on the lower slopes the dominant, root-suckering species of the swamps, *Melaleuca ericifolia*, was invading much of the scrub area. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.

A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.

#### **Materials and Methods**

#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

#### *Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub*

An experimental plot 200 m<sup>2</sup> was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

The vegetation cover and density in the fenced and unfenced plots was assessed by vertical point quadrats using pins 1·5 mm diameter and 2 m tall. In early February, soil was collected from 10 random plots in the same community for examination of seed germination under more favourable conditions of moisture and protection in seed trays placed in the open on a rooftop at the University of Melbourne. #### **Results**

#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*

The classification of the floristic composition of quadrats (10 by 2 m) produced six groups (Fig. 4a) which could be interpreted in relation to topography. Although some groups (I, V) comprised only quadrats from scrub vegetation (Table 1), others (II) were equally distributed between scrub and forest or indicated a distinct preference for one or the other (VI, III). The greatest number of species occurred in forested lower-mid slopes (I), the lowest in wet scrub (IV). Most groups were characterised by gradations of species frequencies although the predominant community in the mid-lower slopes of *Melaleuca-Kunzea-Banksia-Acacia* was distinguished by the high frequency of *Adiantum aethiopicum* in the *Pteridium-Goodenia* field layer. The first two axes of the ordination of the groups (Fig. 4b) accounts for 60% of the quadrat variation. Axis 1 appears to be related loosely to topographic factors such as soil moisture gradients.

#### *Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub*

To allow statistical comparisons of height growth to be made between the transplanted seedlings of the three species in the fencing treatments, it was necessary to pool

the data of all microhabitats because of the low survival in the lighter cover classes. Two-way analyses of variance were performed after logarithmic transformation of each set of measurements. No significant differences between species were observed. However, in 1986 the tallest of the dominant-crowned individuals of *E. muelleriana* (400 cm) far exceeded the tallest *E. obliqua* (256 cm) and *E. baxteri* (285 cm). A longer-term study may show that *E. muelleriana* will come to dominate the site in future years.

The effect of the fencing treatment was significant by April 1980, when all species showed greater height growth (at *P* = 0·05) in the fenced than unfenced plots. Height growth of the eucalypt species in the fenced plots increased markedly in the second and third years, in spite of the severe drought of 1982 (Fig. 8).

The difference in survival between different species of eucalypt during the 6 years of the study were marked. *E. muelleriana* showed consistently higher survival rates than the other species after the first year and *E. obliqua* had the fewest seedlings surviving. After 12 months, only about 20% of the unfenced plants had survived, and after 2 years one plant of *E. muelleriana* remained, and that specimen remained only for an

The pooled data for all species in fenced and unfenced plots are shown in Fig. 9. *E. obliqua* was more severely attacked by groups of sawfly larvae than the other species, and *E. muelleriana* maintained large and horizontally displayed juvenile foliage for at least the second growing season.

The fate of large eucalypt seedlings planted at random in thick scrub and ground stratum in the mid-slope area indicated that plants 1-2 m tall could be located, pulled down and severely browsed, most probably by wallabies. After 3 years, all plants had been destroyed, even those in thick regrowth of *M. ericifolia* and *G. ovata.* The last surviving plant, 2 m tall in 1985, had disappeared without trace 1 year later.

Seeds of the three eucalypt species sown outside fences in mid to late autumn, germinated within 2 weeks and reached the 2-leaf stage and heights of 2-8 cm by the following spring. By December, browsing was evident in four out of 21 plants. By the following autumn all plants had disappeared.

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 11

#### *Regeneration of* A. verticillata *and Other Species in the Scrub*

The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides.* Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea,* but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).

In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata.* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.

The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.

The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea.* Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa, Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea,* may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).

The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer *(Axis porcinus)* are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata,* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea, Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

28	
29	# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*
30	
31	N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡
32	
33	\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, 0-7050 Leipzig, Germany
34	
35	#### Summary
36	
37	1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.
38	
39	2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.
40	
41	3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1-10 years old.
42	
43	4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.
44	
45	5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (≈ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.
46	
47	6 Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V') decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.
48	
49	7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.
50	
51	8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.
52	
53	*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny
54	
55	*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17
56	
57	#### Introduction
58	
59	Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al. 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The
60	
61	Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, Fax: 61 39344 4972, E-mail: Enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au
62	
63	© 1996 British Ecological Society
64	
65	This content downloaded from 209.175.73.10 on Sat, 07 May 2016 01:46:40 UTC
66	All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms
67	
68	
69	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
70	
71	10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*
72	
73	ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).
74	
75	The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.
76	
77	In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).
78	
79	*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).
80	
81	The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski et al. 1994).
82	
83	This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:
84	
85	1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?
86	
87	2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?
88	
89	#### STUDY AREA
90	
91	The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).
92	
93	#### Materials and methods
94	
95	Seven sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.
96	
97

105

Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).
107	
108	For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.
109	
110	Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling et al. 1987).
111	
112	#### STATISTICAL ANALYSES
113	
114	Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.
115	
116	A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') and evenness (V') were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.
117	
118	#### Results
119	
120	#### CONE PRODUCTION
121	
122	A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Plants first produced fertile cones at an age of 5 years. Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.
123	
124	The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).
125	
126	#### SEED PRODUCTION
127	
128	Cones of *Banksia hookeriana* contained up to 20 woody follicles, each of which held two seeds. The maximum possible number of seeds on a plant can

131	
132	Fig. 1 (a) The number of cones produced per year in relation to plant age, and (b) the total number of cones held in the crown in relation to plant age for *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams, Western Australia. Note: standard errors are calculated for the 10 plants which were aged and harvested at the start of the study in 1986, and subsequently for total cones on random sets of 10 plants each year to 1993.

# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*

N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, 0-7050 Leipzig, Germany

#### Summary

1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1-10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (≈ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.

6 Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V') decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny

*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17

#### Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al. 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The

10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*

ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).

The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.

In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).

*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).

The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski et al. 1994).

This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:

1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?

2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?

#### STUDY AREA

The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).

#### Materials and methods

Seven sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.
